summaries.example: Imagine you lend a classmate your favorite book. You may have a privilege to use your own book, a claim that your classmate return it, and a power to give the book away. Your classmate may have a duty to return it. These different parts can fit together to make one property right.
summaries.summary: A right is an entitlement. It can mean that someone is allowed to act, that another person must act or leave them alone, that someone has authority to change a rule, or that others are not allowed to change the person’s situation. Philosophers sort rights into categories, such as moral, legal, customary, human, children’s, or property rights. They also study how rights are built. A right to a bicycle, for example, may include permission to use it, a claim that others not take it, a power to lend or sell it, and protection against someone changing the ownership without permission. Rights can be active, concerning what the holder does, or passive, concerning what others must or must not do. They can also be negative, requiring non-interference, or positive, requiring some good or service. The entry explains disagreements about the purpose of rights. One view says rights give people control over duties. Another says rights protect important interests. Other approaches connect rights with demands, relationships, or several different functions. Rights matter because they distribute freedom and authority, but their exact limits and justification remain debated.
key_ideas: Rights can concern actions, protection, property, freedom, or services.
A claim by one person usually matches a duty held by someone else.
Rights have different parts: privileges, claims, powers, and immunities.
Some rights protect us from interference; others call for help or services.
Rights help organize laws, governments, and ideas about fairness.
Philosophers disagree about why rights exist and who or what can have them.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rights affect everyday rules and major institutions. They help explain why someone may use property, speak freely, receive protection, or ask for assistance. Studying rights also teaches us to ask exactly what an entitlement requires, who has a duty, and whether a right can be limited. Careful thinking is useful when rights appear to conflict or when a proposed right would place serious responsibilities on other people.

important_terms.definition: An entitlement: a special permission, protection, or authority someone has.
A permission to do something because you have no duty not to do it.
An entitlement that means another person has a duty toward you.
An ability to change rules, permissions, or duties, such as by promising or giving permission.
Protection against someone else changing your rights or duties in a certain way.
The person or group that has a right.

questions_to_think_about: How is having permission different from being owed something?
Can a person have a right even if they cannot speak up for it?
Should every right be protected in exactly the same way?
When might two people’s rights seem to point in different directions?

summaries.example: Consider a student’s right to a fair hearing in a school discipline case. The student may have a claim that officials follow a fair procedure, while officials have a directed duty owed to that student. The student may also have an immunity against a particular official changing the procedure arbitrarily. The school board may possess a power to create or alter disciplinary rules, but that power can itself be limited by higher rules. This shows why a single right may contain several connected incidents rather than one simple permission.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of rights asks both what rights are and what they do. Hohfeld’s analytical framework treats familiar rights as structured combinations of four incidents. A privilege means that the holder has no duty not to act. A claim correlates with a duty owed by another. A power is an ability to alter normative relations, as in promising, consenting, transferring property, or making legal rules. An immunity exists when another party lacks a relevant power over the holder. These incidents have logical opposites and correlatives, and they can form complex, layered rights. The framework also clarifies distinctions between active and passive rights and between negative and positive rights, though the latter distinction does not map onto every kind of right and may obscure the resources needed for enforcement. The harder question concerns function. Will theories identify rights with control over duties; interest theories identify them with the protection of interests or well-being. Each explains some cases and faces problems with others, including unwaivable rights, rights of children and animals, bare privileges, and official powers. Further debates concern directed duties, rights’ special normative force, apparent conflicts, rights to do wrong, and the possible holders of rights. Finally, the entry surveys status-based, instrumental, and contractual approaches to justifying rights, along with critiques that rights language can overemphasize isolated individuals or hide effects on duty-bearers and communities.
key_ideas: Hohfeld’s system distinguishes privileges, claims, powers, and immunities, along with their logical opposites and correlatives.
Complex or “molecular” rights combine several basic incidents and may include first-order and higher-order elements.
Active rights concern the holder’s own action; passive rights regulate what others do. Negative rights concern non-interference, while positive rights concern provision.
The will theory emphasizes normative control, but has difficulty explaining unwaivable rights and rights held by infants or animals.
The interest theory accommodates incapable right-holders more easily, but must explain why every protected interest is not automatically a right.
Justifications for rights may be status-based, instrumental, or contractual, and critics question whether rights language is too individualistic or obscures burdens on others.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rights are not merely labels for preferred outcomes. They structure legal authority, political constitutions, moral claims, and the distribution of freedom. Analyzing a right reveals who may act, who must act, who may change the rules, and who is protected from change. Theories of rights also shape disagreements about liberty, welfare, property, equality, and institutional power. Understanding the competing theories makes it possible to evaluate both rights-based arguments and criticisms of “rights talk” without assuming that every assertion of a right has the same form or force.

important_terms.definition: An entitlement involving permission, a duty owed to someone, authority to alter normative relations, or protection from such alteration.
A Hohfeldian incident in which an agent has no duty not to perform an action.
A Hohfeldian incident that correlates with another party’s duty owed to the right-holder.
Normative authority to alter one’s own or another person’s privileges, claims, powers, or immunities.
Protection that exists because another party lacks the power to alter the holder’s normative position in a specified way.
A duty owed specifically to a right-holder, whose breach may wrong that person rather than merely violate a general duty.
The view that rights function chiefly by giving holders control over others’ duties.
The view that rights function chiefly by protecting or advancing the interests or well-being of their holders or their kind.

questions_to_think_about: Does a right require the holder to be able to waive or exercise it?
Are positive rights fundamentally different from negative rights, or do both require social institutions and resources to enforce them?
When a right appears to conflict with another right, should one right be specified more narrowly, or can a right be defeated while still leaving a reason for apology or compensation?
Should a theory of rights focus on the holder’s control, the holder’s interests, or the relationships created by duties?
What features, if any, make humans, animals, groups, or institutions possible right-holders?

summaries.example: Suppose your class agrees that everyone may use the basketball court during lunch. You have a privilege to play because you have no rule forbidding you. You may also have a claim that other students do not push you off the court, which gives those students a duty. If the class captain can change the schedule, the captain has a power. If the captain is not allowed to cancel your turn without following the rules, you have an immunity. One everyday “right” can therefore contain several different parts.
summaries.summary: Rights are entitlements, but entitlements take different forms. A person may be permitted to act, owed protection or assistance, empowered to change a rule, or protected from another authority changing their position. Philosophers classify rights by their holders, their objects, their sources, and whether they can be waived or lost. They also use Hohfeld’s system to analyze the internal structure of rights. Privileges and powers concern what the holder can do; claims and immunities mainly regulate what others can do. A complicated right, such as ownership, may combine all four. The entry distinguishes negative rights, which involve non-interference, from positive rights, which involve provision, while noting that enforcing either kind can require public resources. It then examines theories about the purpose of rights. Will theorists connect rights with control over other people’s duties. Interest theorists connect them with protecting well-being, though interests do not always seem sufficient to create rights. Other accounts emphasize what people can demand, the value of relationships, or several functions rather than one. Philosophers also ask why rights have special weight, whether rights really conflict, whether someone can have a right to do something wrong, and which beings can hold rights. Theories that justify rights appeal to human status, beneficial consequences, or fair agreement. Critics reply that rights may encourage individualism or hide burdens placed on others and communities.
key_ideas: Rights come in many categories: legal, moral, customary, human, children’s, workers’, property, and others.
The Hohfeldian system shows that “having a right” can mean more than simply having permission.
A claim and a duty are correlatives: if one person has a claim, someone else has a duty owed to them.
Negative rights involve freedom from interference, while positive rights involve receiving goods or services; both may require institutions to enforce them.
The will theory stresses control over duties, while the interest theory stresses protection of well-being.
Rights can be justified by a person’s status, by useful consequences, or by principles people could reasonably agree to.
summaries.why_it_matters: Knowing the structure of a right helps us avoid vague arguments. If someone says, “I have a right,” we can ask: Is this permission, a claim on another person, authority to change a rule, or protection against authority? We can also ask where the right comes from and what duties it creates. These questions matter in schools, courts, governments, and moral disagreements because different rights may have different holders, strengths, limits, and responsibilities.

important_terms.definition: An entitlement that gives someone permission, protection, authority, or an expectation that another person must act.
A permission to act that means the person has no duty not to perform that action.
A right that matches a duty owed by another person or group.
Authority to create, remove, transfer, or change rights and duties.
A safeguard against another person or institution changing your rights in a particular way.
The person or group whose right creates a duty for someone else.
A duty aimed at a particular person, so breaking it may wrong that person.
A theory that says rights mainly protect important interests or well-being.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a right to speak include protection from interference as well as permission to speak?
Can someone have a right that they cannot give up? What would a will theorist say?
Does having an interest in something automatically give someone a right to it?
Why might a legal right and a moral right point in different directions?
Should rights always belong to individuals, or can groups and institutions hold them too?
